lines.text: A pretrained Transformer learns two things: representations, and a rule for comparing them.
When we fine-tune, we usually change the representations.
The rule that decides which tokens attend to which is simply inherited.
Take one query and seven keys, and hold them fixed.
Under the dot product, attention goes to B, furthest along the query’s direction.
With Euclidean distance, the nearest key, A, wins.
Taxicab distance picks D.
An anisotropic metric picks F.
Nothing moved. Only the geometry changed.
GeoAFT makes that geometry trainable.
It keeps the pretrained score and adds a small structured term, like a learned L-p distance or a Mahalanobis metric.
Its gate starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the pretrained model.
We first tested it on synthetic targets with a known relation.
GeoAFT recovered over ninety-nine point nine percent of the oracle gap on both targets.
That is about forty points ahead of Q/K LoRA, and six to twelve points ahead of tested generic scorers.
Not every registered comparison passed: a fixed L-p bank came almost as close.
On a nonlinear target, 46 trainable parameters fit about as well as the tested 8,705-parameter MLP: an economy, not a clear win.
But theory adds a twist.
A Mahalanobis geometry is exactly a bilinear score plus a key-dependent bias: a known score family, not new capacity.
So geometry adaptation is not uniformly better.
Some updates are exact reparameterizations, some are more economical, and some may add new capacity.
Telling these apart is the real question. So far, the evidence is controlled and synthetic.
When should adaptation change representations, and when should it change how they relate?
More on the QRS website.
